VIII.1.title: Three times declined
VIII.1.reflection: Taibo, eldest son of an early Zhou lord, three times gave up his claim to the throne so that a younger line could rule, and did it so quietly that the people had nothing to praise. Confucius calls this the highest virtue. Goodness that leaves no mark to applaud is put at the top.
VIII.1.question: What good could you do today that no one would know to thank you for?

VIII.2.title: Virtues without ritual
VIII.2.reflection: Respect without ritual becomes tiresome, caution becomes timidity, courage becomes disorder, frankness becomes rudeness. Each good quality needs a form to hold it in shape. The second half adds that when those above are devoted to their families and do not forget old friends, the people follow.
VIII.2.question: Which of your good qualities turns into a fault when it has no form?

VIII.3.title: As if on thin ice
VIII.3.reflection: Dying, Master Zeng asks his students to uncover his hands and feet: his body, received from his parents, is whole. He quotes the Odes on walking as if on the edge of an abyss, as if on thin ice, and says that from now on he knows he is free of that care. Keeping the body unharmed was, for him, part of filial piety.
VIII.3.question: What have you been carrying carefully all your life, and why?

VIII.4.title: A dying man's words
VIII.4.reflection: When a bird is about to die its cry is sad; when a man is about to die his words are good. Master Zeng then tells the visiting noble three things that matter: bearing without violence, a face close to sincerity, speech without coarseness. The ritual vessels, he adds, have their own officers. He sends the great man back to his own conduct.
VIII.4.question: If you had only three things to tell someone in power, what would they be?

VIII.5.title: My old friend
VIII.5.reflection: Able, yet asking those less able; rich in knowledge, yet asking those who have little; having, as if not having; full, as if empty; wronged, and not disputing it: Master Zeng once had a friend like this. Tradition takes the friend to be Yan Hui.
VIII.5.question: Which of these five do you find hardest?

VIII.6.title: Entrusted with an orphan
VIII.6.reflection: Someone who can be entrusted with a young orphan prince and the government of a state, and who cannot be moved in a great crisis: is this a junzi? Yes, a junzi. Master Zeng defines the junzi by trustworthiness under pressure.
VIII.6.question: What would you trust to someone only if you were sure they could not be moved?

VIII.7.title: A heavy load, a long road
VIII.7.reflection: The scholar must be broad and resolute, for the load is heavy and the road long. Ren is the load: is that not heavy? Only death ends the road: is that not long? Master Zeng's picture of the moral life has no finish line before the last.
VIII.7.question: What load have you taken on that will last as long as you do?

VIII.8.title: Odes, ritual, music
VIII.8.reflection: One is roused by the Odes, established by ritual, and completed by music. Three arts and three stages: feeling, form, harmony. Education here is aesthetic as much as moral.
VIII.8.question: Which art first roused you?

VIII.9.title: Made to follow
VIII.9.reflection: The people can be made to follow, not made to understand. The chapter is often read as contempt for ordinary people, and it can be. It can also be read as a statement of fact about government: example moves people further than explanation. A different punctuation of the Chinese, proposed by some scholars, makes it say: let them follow if they can, and if not, teach them.
VIII.9.question: Have you ever followed someone well without understanding why?

VIII.10.title: Driven to disorder
VIII.10.reflection: A bold man who hates poverty will make trouble; so will a man without ren if he is hated too much. The second clause is the surprising one: excessive dislike of the bad can itself breed disorder.
VIII.10.question: Whom do you dislike so much that it might make things worse?

VIII.11.title: Proud and mean
VIII.11.reflection: Even with the talents of the Duke of Zhou, if a person is proud and stingy, the rest is not worth looking at. The Duke was Confucius's model statesman. Talent cannot redeem arrogance and meanness.
VIII.11.question: What talent of yours might be cancelled by a habit you do not see?

VIII.12.title: Three years of study
VIII.12.reflection: It is hard to find someone who has studied three years without thinking of a salary. Legge reads the end differently, as "without coming to be good". The usual modern reading is the salary one, which fits II.18.
VIII.12.question: When did you last learn something without thinking of what it would earn you?

VIII.13.title: Ashamed of poverty, ashamed of riches
VIII.13.reflection: Hold firmly to good faith and love learning; keep to the good Way until death. Do not enter a state in danger or stay in one in disorder; show yourself when the world has the Way and hide when it does not. When the state has the Way, to be poor is shameful; when it lacks the Way, to be rich is shameful.
VIII.13.question: In the world as it is now, what kind of success would be shameful?

VIII.14.title: Not in the office
VIII.14.reflection: One who does not hold the office does not plan its policy. The sentence is plain about responsibility: authority and the right to decide come together. It returns in XIV.26.
VIII.14.question: Where are you deciding things that are not your responsibility?

VIII.15.title: How it filled the ears
VIII.15.reflection: When the music master Zhi began, the finale of the Guanju flooded the ears. A memory of a performance, recorded with pleasure. The book has room for a concert remembered.
VIII.15.question: What performance do you still remember in your ears?

VIII.16.title: I do not understand them
VIII.16.reflection: Ardent but not upright, ignorant but not careful, simple but not honest: such people Confucius does not understand. Each pair joins a weakness to the absence of the virtue that usually comes with it.
VIII.16.question: What combination in people puzzles you most?

VIII.17.title: As if you could not reach it
VIII.17.reflection: Study as if you cannot catch up, and still fear losing what you have. The urgency of learning in two directions: forward, and holding on.
VIII.17.question: What are you afraid of losing that you once learned?

VIII.18.title: As if it were nothing
VIII.18.reflection: How sublime Shun and Yu were: they held the whole world and it was as if it were nothing to them. Possession without attachment is the mark of the sage kings.
VIII.18.question: What do you possess that you could hold more lightly?

VIII.19.title: The greatness of Yao
VIII.19.reflection: Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modelled himself on it. His virtue was so vast the people had no name for it; his achievements and his culture shone. The chapter praises the first of the sage kings in the language of awe.
VIII.19.question: Whom do you admire so much that words for it run out?

VIII.20.title: Talent is hard to find
VIII.20.reflection: Shun had five ministers; King Wu said he had ten. Confucius notes how rare talent is, adding, in Legge's reading, that one of the ten was a woman, so the able ministers were only nine men. The chapter's point is the rarity of talent; the way it counts shows the assumption of its world, that office belonged to men, while still naming the woman among the ten. It ends by praising the Zhou for still serving the Shang when they held two thirds of the realm.
VIII.20.question: Whose talent around you goes uncounted because of who they are?

VIII.21.title: No flaw in Yu
VIII.21.reflection: Yu the Great, who tamed the floods, ate simply but was generous to the spirits, dressed plainly but wore fine robes at sacrifice, lived in a low house but spent his strength on the irrigation channels. Confucius can find no fault. Private frugality, public generosity.
VIII.21.question: Where do you spend on yourself what should go to the common good?
